https://www.dw.com/en/south-korea-16-dea.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5IE7O Authorities have issued a heatwave warning for Seoul Image: Jung Yeon-je/AFP Advertisement At least 16 people have died in South Korea , as a record heatwave hits the country. President Lee Jae Myung has called for increased support for those affected amid warnings that extreme weather was becoming more frequent. Between May 15 and August 2 this year, a total of 2,025 people have suffered heat-related illnesses, the interior ministry said in a statement. What did President Lee say? "We need to make efforts for a fundamental overhaul of the national crisis system, ​since this extreme weather is becoming normal ," President Lee said at a cabinet meeting, where he urged officials to accelerate measures to protect the daily lives of people . He also called for inspections of ‌power systems as demand for air ‌conditioning rises. South Korea's southeastern island city of Yangsan recorded a temperature of 42.5 degrees Celsius (108.5 degrees Fahrenheit) on ‌Sunday, the highest measured in 122 years of ​observations, the national weather agency said. President Lee Jae Myung urged officials to increase support for those affected as extreme weather becomes more frequent. Image: Kim Hong-ji/REUTERS After authorities issued their first-ever heatwave warning ⁠for parts of Seoul and Gyeonggi on Monday, the Korea Meteorological Administration extended it to the entire capital city on Tuesday. This was the first such advisory since the designation was introduced this year to alert the public about extreme temperatures. South Korea grapples with historic heat wave Temperatures in the capital hit 38 degrees Celsius at midday and were expected to fall only to about 29 degrees overnight. Residents were urged to stay indoors and drink plenty of water. The city has also designated about 4,000 public facilities as cooling centers. While Seoul has a population of 9.6 million people, the wider metropolitan area is home to more than 25 million residents, which is about half of the country's population. Scientists have warned that extreme weather events like heat waves are becoming increasingly frequent and more intense as a result of climate change . Tama Zoo in Tokyo announced Tuesday that three lions have died in the past week due to suspected complications from heatstroke as Japan swelters. Europe has also faced a sweltering summer, with Germany's heat-related death toll for 2026 already surpassing every full-year total since 2016 — and expected to climb as another spell of extreme temperatures takes hold. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: A firefighter battles flames as the Timber fire burns in Big Sur, California, on 10 August 2026. Photograph: Tayfun Coskun/Anadolu via Getty Images View image in fullscreen A firefighter battles flames as the Timber fire burns in Big Sur, California, on 10 August 2026. Photograph: Tayfun Coskun/Anadolu via Getty Images California Famed tourist destinations evacuated as wildfire threatens California’s Big Sur Nearly 500 personnel battle Timber fire in Los Padres national forest as blaze grows to 2,000 acres Dani Anguiano and agency Tue 11 Aug 2026 12.22 EDT First published on Tue 11 Aug 2026 09.53 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Evacuations have been ordered for areas along California’s famous Big Sur coast as a wildfire burns in the nearby steep, rugged mountains. The Timber fire in Monterey county started on Sunday and grew to 2,000 acres by Tuesday morning, according to Cal Fire, the state’s fire agency. Nearly 500 fire personnel had been assigned to the fire in the Los Padres national forest. The evacuations have affected famed tourist destinations such as the Nepenthe restaurant, the Henry Miller Memorial Library and the Alila Ventana resort, as well as state parks during the region’s busiest season. Part of the Pacific Coast Highway was closed for non-residents, and officials urged visitors to avoid the area entirely. ‘Unprecedented, dangerous territory’: US north-west reckons with a summer of historic wildfires Read more Firefighters worked to build containment lines along the Highway 1 corridor, Cal Fire said on Monday, and have boxed in 5% of the blaze. Ground crews are working to access difficult terrain, the agency said, but the fire is moving slowly, burning primarily along the ground through grass, brush and oak woodland and has not moved into the tree tops. Officials said they are focused on protecting area homes and keeping the fire from moving across the Pacific Coast Highway. The cause of the fire, which started on Saturday evening and now threatens 259 buildings, is still under investigation. Firefighters are fighting blazes across the US west. Canada put its military on standby on Monday to help battle deadly wildfires in British Columbia, where at least one woman has died and about 20,000 people have fled their homes. Nearly half of the fires in the region are burning out of control, according to authorities. The mayor of Summerland – home to about 12,000 people, which was ordered evacuated on Saturday night along with about 8,000 people in and around nearby Peachland – warned that the affected areas remained too dangerous to enter and that it was impossible to determine the scope of the destruction. Meanwhile, a quick-moving blaze just north of Reno, Nevada, forced about 5,500 people to evacuate. Firefighters in Spokane, Washington, strengthened containment lines around three destructive blazes in that state, allowing some evacuated residents to return home. And Oregon is experiencing its worst year on record for land burned by large wildfires, with 3,671 sq miles (9,508 sq km) scorched, said Jean Nelson-Dean, spokesperson for Northwest Interagency Coordination Center. That beats the state’s previous record set in 2024. In the foothills of California’s Sierra Nevada, firefighters have contained 90% of the Gann fire, which killed one person and destroyed 48 structures. Investigators have said the blaze was sparked by a man using a chainsaw, and arrested him last week. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Victorian premier Ben Carroll has called a royal commission into the construction sector, which will examine allegations of corruption among the CFMEU and others connected to the Big Build. Photograph: James Ross/AAP View image in fullscreen Victorian premier Ben Carroll has called a royal commission into the construction sector, which will examine allegations of corruption among the CFMEU and others connected to the Big Build. Photograph: James Ross/AAP Victorian politics ‘There was grift, there was thuggery’: Victorian premier says ‘nothing is off limits’ at construction royal commission Ben Carroll releases terms of reference for inquiry that will include examining allegations of CFMEU corruption on state government building sites Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Benita Kolovos Victorian state correspondent Thu 20 Aug 2026 01.47 EDT First published on Wed 19 Aug 2026 21.06 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google “Nothing is off limits” to Victoria’s royal commission into the construction sector, Ben Carroll has said, as he released the inquiry’s terms of reference and confirmed former premiers and ministers could be called to face public hearings. The Victorian premier on Thursday unveiled details of the inquiry – while acknowledging there had been “grift”, “thuggery” and “violence” on taxpayer-funded building sites – after the governor signed the letters patent formally establishing the commission earlier in the morning. Chris Kourakis, the former chief justice of South Australia, whom Carroll described as “independent, rigorous and fearless”, has been appointed commissioner. Victoria moves to expand definition of ‘corruption’ before state election Read more Kourakis, who has been given coercive powers to compel the production of information, including cabinet documents, and the attendance of witnesses, has been given a $50m budget and must report to the government by 20 August 2027. The inquiry has been formally named the Royal Commission into the Integrity of Major Public and Civil Infrastructure Construction Projects in Victoria. Carroll said the inquiry followed allegations of wrongdoing by the CFMEU and others connected to the Big Build , first reported by Nine newspapers in 2024. “It is clear – and I want to acknowledge the role of both investigative journalism and whistleblowers – that there was grift, there was thuggery, there was misogyny, and there was violence on taxpayer-funded construction sites. I have zero tolerance for that,” he told reporters. “We are giving this royal commission the broadest, most extensive, wide-ranging powers: full transparency, nothing is off limits. “Victorians deserve answers, and this royal commission will provide them.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Under the terms of reference, the commission will investigate the extent to which “corruption, criminal conduct or serious misconduct” occurred on major Victorian projects by the Construction, Forestry and Maritime Employees Union (CFMEU), construction companies, subcontractors, labour hire firms and others. It will also examine whether government departments and project delivery agencies “adequately adhered” to their responsibilities in overseeing the projects. The inquiry will consider whether measures could be taken to “recoup” taxpayer funds that were “misappropriated or received as a result of corruption, criminal conduct or serious misconduct”. Download original document However, “lawful, legitimate and appropriate actions taken” under industrial relations and occupational health and safety laws are outside the inquiry’s scope. The commission can examine whether those laws or regulations were misused. Carroll said the terms of reference make it a matter for the commissioner to decide whose actions and knowledge are relevant to the matters under investigation. “Not the government, not me. The commissioner,” he said. “If he wants to hear from ministers, former ministers, senior officials, union leaders or company executives, he has the power to call them.” Under questioning, he confirmed “premiers and former premiers” can also be called. He also confirmed their legal representation – and that of former ministers – will be publicly funded, which he described as “standard procedure”. The shadow attorney general, James Newbury, said Carroll should “guarantee” both Jacinta Allan and Daniel Andrews would be “hauled before this commission” prior to the November election. Newbury also described Carroll’s decision to establish the royal commission as a “political fix minutes before the election”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion Carroll denied he was driven by self-interest, saying: “This is about the future of our state and valuing taxpayer dollars.” In a short statement, Kourakis said he was “deeply conscious of the responsibility with which I have been entrusted” and said the royal commission will undertake its work “independently and rigorously”. “We will follow the evidence and ensure our processes are fair, thorough, and transparent,” he said. The CFMEU administrator, Michael Crosby, said in a statement it would “fully cooperate” with the royal commission. He said while “significant public attention” had been focused on the union, “misconduct is not confined to one organisation”. Crosby urged the commission to also examine “the conduct of developers, head contractors, subcontractors, labour hire operators and anyone else who has profited from unlawful or unethical behaviour”. “The CFMEU has been calling out wage theft, sham contracting, phoenixing, safety breaches and the exploitation of vulnerable workers for years now. These practices rob workers of their pay, put lives at risk and undermine honest businesses doing the right thing,” he said. “Governments, law enforcement and regulators must shine the spotlight across the entire industry. Victorian workers deserve nothing less.” Carroll’s first act as premier three weeks ago was to announce he would set up the inquiry into the sector. Carroll also said a special prosecutor would be appointed to work in parallel to the royal commission, and that the Independent Broad-based Anti-corruption Commission would be bolstered with follow-the-money powers. Both these elements would require legislation, which he had committed to introducing to parliament before the government enters caretaker mode before the November state election. It is understood Victorian parliament will sit for additional days to allow for this to occur. Allan, Carroll’s predecessor, was the minister responsible for transport infrastructure at the time when most alleged wrongdoing occurred. While she apologised for criminal allegations that had been uncovered, she had rejected calls for a royal commission, which put her at odds with a number of her MPs . It led several to join a cross-factional group that urged Carroll to challenge Allan for the leadership. She stood down before a vote. https://www.politico.eu/article/giorgia-.text: ROME — One date has always loomed large in Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s political calendar: Friday, Sept. 4. As she gathers with her allies for a jamboree in the southern port city of Bari, Meloni will overtake Silvio Berlusconi’s record for the longest unbroken stretch running a government in the history of the Italian Republic: 1,412 days. The big question — with a general election due next year — is how far Meloni’s right-wing dominance of Italy’s politics will endure. She still has a long way to go to rival Berlusconi’s total of 3,340 days in charge across all his mandates. Advertisement Advertisement Berlusconi’s extraordinary endurance rested on his ability to survive electoral defeats, collapsed governments, criminal trials and repeated predictions of his political death. His wealth, television empire and a party constructed around himself gave him resources independent of his popularity at any particular moment. Meloni lacks those tycoon-style advantages, but she is still only 49 years old, tops the polls and is planning an electoral reform that could make it easier for her to keep her grip on power. Nearly four years after taking office, she towers over her coalition partners without an obvious challenger on the right. Italo Bocchino, a former conservative parliamentarian and prominent Meloni supporter, predicted her era “will last 30 years” — even if some of those years are in opposition. Her appeal, he argued, lies in her unfiltered authenticity: She complains in dialect about high heels and needing the toilet at international summits and press conferences, embraces her “fishwife” nickname and is notorious for eye-rolls that betray what she is thinking. “She is sincere, she is transparent as glass,” he said. Her image as a petite blonde woman, Bocchino argued, also made a leader from Italy’s post-fascist right appear less threatening to wary voters. On the other side of the political spectrum, Laura Boldrini, a center-left Democratic Party MP and former speaker of the lower house, insisted Meloni had not yet earned the comparison with Berlusconi. Advertisement Advertisement “I don’t think she will last a long time because she has failed,” she said. “I think the results are very modest and very disappointing for those who supported her and voted for her.” Meloni’s opponents accuse her of failing to revive the country’s stagnant economy and low wages and of wasting money on futile efforts to reduce migration. Critics say she focused her efforts on measures intended to cement her power, such as electoral reform and a failed shakeup of the judiciary, while failing to tackle a cost of living crisis. Boldrini argued that the rise of former General Roberto Vannacci as a force on the far right also showed that disillusioned right-wing voters were already looking elsewhere. Silvio Berlusconi at the Italy-France Summit on April 26, 2011 in Rome, Italy. | Giorgio Cosulich/Getty Images “The right-wing coalition has a big problem called Vannacci: a fascist, racist, misogynist, who is collecting a lot of resentment from those who have been disappointed by Meloni’s government. They say they won’t run together but I think they will or they won’t win,” she said. More credible than Silvio On the international stage, Meloni has established far more credibility than her predecessor Berlusconi. While Berlusconi cultivated allies across the political spectrum, from Russia’s Vladimir Putin to Britain’s Tony Blair, his gaffes, Bunga Bunga parties and sex scandals frequently made him an object of ridicule abroad. Meloni is regarded as a pragmatist at European summits and has built strong relationships with European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. Advertisement Advertisement Berlusconi, by contrast, had a bumpy relationship with then German Chancellor Angela Merkel. Meloni has also proved successful in pulling the EU closer to positions she has advocated on migration, trade deals, industry and green policy. Four years of political stability under her leadership have themselves increased Italy’s weight abroad, analysts argue. That influence is now being tested, however, as Germany, Ireland and several other European countries press Italy to take back asylum seekers who first entered the EU there under the bloc’s new migration rules, reopening an old fault line between Italy and northern European governments. Lorenzo Pregliasco, a political analyst and pollster, said voters continue to give Meloni credit for her stewardship of the government and her handling of international affairs. “She is seen as fit to be prime minister in a way other party leaders maybe are not.” Roberto D’Alimonte, a political scientist who has compared Meloni to Merkel, said: “She has become the center of gravity for the right,” adding that “there is no alternative leader in that coalition.” But whether that dominance can survive a more uncertain political landscape is only beginning to be tested. Advertisement Advertisement Much of the vote of her party, Brothers of Italy, comes from volatile center-right voters who have previously moved between parties. Meloni also faces growing economic headwinds. The economy is forecast to enter recession later this year and Italy is on course to overtake Greece as Europe’s most indebted country. With energy prices high and pressure mounting to increase defense spending, she has little room for generous handouts to shore up support in her final pre-election budget this autumn. Friedrich Merz, Donald Trump, Antonio Costa and Meloni at a work lunch as part of the G7 summit, in Evian, France, on June 16, 2026. | Pool photo by Christian Hartmann/AFP via Getty Images Her coalition partners have meanwhile lost ground to Vannacci’s new force, leaving a united left potentially competitive if it can agree on a program and candidate before the election. Meloni may ultimately be forced to bring an unruly Vannacci inside the tent. Next stop: the presidency? For Pregliasco, Meloni has yet to have the overarching impact of Berlusconi, who created the modern center-right coalition in 1994 and helped reshape Italian politics around his highly personalized leadership. Meloni has so far inherited and dominated that architecture rather than creating her own. “I wouldn’t consider her as defining a figure as Berlusconi,” Pregliasco said. Advertisement Advertisement That could yet change. Meloni’s majority is pursuing an electoral reform that would replace single-member constituencies with proportional representation and award a bonus to the winning coalition, potentially giving her a more commanding majority if the center-right wins again. That approach closely echoes Berlusconi’s 2005 reform, which also combined proportional representation with a majority bonus. A second term with a reinforced parliamentary majority could strengthen her hand in the 2029 election of the president of the Republic and could allow her to revive her stalled plans for the direct election of the prime minister. Neither would be straightforward: constitutional reform remains politically hazardous, while the president is elected by secret ballot. But success would give Meloni the opportunity to leave a more lasting institutional mark by reshaping the political system herself. Her ambitions may also not end with a long tenure as premier. Nicola Procaccini, a senior politician from Brothers of Italy who has known Meloni since their time in youth politics, said she could ultimately climb to the venerated role of president. He explained that after three decades in public life, Italians know both her strengths and flaws. “She is not a leader by chance,” he said. “Everyone knows what to expect from her.” Advertisement Paradoxically, Berlusconi’s death in 2023 made Meloni’s task easier by removing a potentially troublesome figure with pro-Russian sympathies who was deeply reluctant to play second fiddle to a much younger woman from her coalition. Procaccini sees Meloni remaining a political force for decades, although he laughed at the idea that she would want another 20 or 30 years in the prime minister’s office. The job, performed with her level of intensity, was “grueling,” he said. But as Meloni’s followers prepare to toast her success in Bari, Boldrini was unimpressed by the record itself. “Longevity is not a value per se, ” she cautioned. “You have to implement policies that improve people’s lives, make reforms and make a difference. And this hasn’t happened.” Advertisement

https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/s.text: Left to right: SNP leader John Swinney, Plaid Cymru leader Rhun ap Iorweth, Sinn Féin president Mary Lou McDonald and Northern Ireland first minister Michelle O'Neill. Photograph: Jon Rowley/EPA View image in fullscreen Left to right: SNP leader John Swinney, Plaid Cymru leader Rhun ap Iorweth, Sinn Féin president Mary Lou McDonald and Northern Ireland first minister Michelle O'Neill. Photograph: Jon Rowley/EPA First Edition newsletter Wales Tuesday briefing: How to understand Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland’s joint call for change In today’s newsletter: Plaid Cymru, the SNP and Sinn Féin have signed an agreement for greater powers, as pressure grows on Westminster over the UK’s future Libby Brooks Tue 15 Sep 2026 01.45 EDT Last modified on Tue 15 Sep 2026 01.47 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Good morning. Back in May, the shape of British politics shifted dramatically. I’ll forgive you if you were too preoccupied refreshing Andrew Sparrow’s live blog for the latest speculation about Keir Starmer to notice, but since 7 May, centre-left nationalist parties that ultimately aspire to leave the UK have been in government for the first time simultaneously in Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland . This week sees the initial codification of that shift. In Cardiff yesterday, Plaid Cymru leader Rhun ap Iorwerth, Scottish National party leader John Swinney and Sinn Féin vice-president Michelle O’Neill (who shares power with the Democratic Unionist party) affirmed their countries’ right to seek independence from the UK. Along with the leader of the opposition in Ireland, Mary Lou McDonald, they signed a memorandum of understanding that called on Westminster “to prepare, plan and facilitate constitutional change in Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland”. And they posed for a fair number of group photos too. With each of the sister parties having a different timeline towards a referendum and its own domestic pressures, it’s tempting to dismiss this as spectacle over substance. However, these first ministers are not shouting into a vacuum. They are part of a cross-national conversation in which devolution is the defining project of the UK’s still newish prime minister. For today’s First Edition, I spoke to our Wales correspondent, Bethan McKernan , in Cardiff about why this agreement is more than a photocall, and checked in with colleagues in Scotland and Ireland for the view from there too. But first, the headlines. Five big stories Reform UK | Andy Burnham’s government could thwart Reform’s unprecedented £72m donations with retrospective restrictions on political donors that will include tough new residency requirements, ministers have announced. AI | Donald Trump has dismissed calls to increase controls on AI as a “sick conspiracy”, as stocks linked to the technology slumped after appeals from Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX leaders on the weekend for the industry to slow down. Nato | Nato fighter jets shot down a drone over Lithuania after an alert was issued in the ‌capital and surrounding region, while Poland scrambled fighter jets less than a day after retrieving a suspected Russian drone adrift in its waters. Middle East | Yemen’s Houthi rebels have seized two strategic islands in the Red Sea, reinforcing the Iran-backed group’s ability to control a key shipping route, as concerns mount that the world is facing a new oil supply crisis. Lucy Letby | Two leading experts have quit Lucy Letby’s defence team over concerns about the “scientific credibility” of some of its evidence. In depth: Can devolution hold the UK together? View image in fullscreen Andy Burnham has made devolution a central part of his political agenda, but the rise of nationalist governments across the UK presents a challenge to his vision. Photograph: Adrian Weston/Alamy Listening to the leaders in Cardiff discuss the “growing recognition that Westminster is not working” and that “power genuinely needs to be brought closer to people and communities”, you might have thought Andy Burnham was in the room. The memorandum signed by all four stated that no Westminster government has the right to “block democracy” by refusing a referendum should the public demand it. At the morning press conference Swinney and O’Neill called for immediate referendums in Scotland and Northern Ireland; ap Iorwerth declined to give a timetable. Later that afternoon, the Scottish and Welsh first ministers signed the Cardiff Agreement, setting out shared priorities like child poverty and economic growth, and which Swinney described as “an important moment in the history of devolution”. Events in Cardiff were gifted extra salience by a series of unscripted interventions over the past week. On a visit to Ireland last weekend, Donald Trump told reporters that he would “love” to see a united Ireland and it “may as well happen now”, prompting swift rebuttal from unionists on the Stormont executive and the UK government, as well as a solid gold response from SDLP leader Claire Hanna, who said: “It turns out that he isn’t as orange as he looks”. Only weeks prior, Andy Burnham incensed Irish nationalists by declaring a reunification referendum was “off the table” – forgetting that it’s not his table, because the Good Friday agreement includes a provision for a border poll should it appear that the majority of Northern Irish voters want to leave the UK. In a constitutional one-two, Burnham said last week at PMQs that a second referendum on Scottish independence could be held if a “clear consensus” emerged in favour - but swiftly self-corrected, telling an eager Swinney that such a vote was “off-limits” while he focuses on growing the economy and tackling the cost of living. Nonetheless, says Bethan McKernan, “there is this sense that since Plaid Cymru won the Senedd elections in Wales in May, this is a new chapter in the Celtic struggle for independence – or breaking up the UK, depending on which way you look at it.” What this all means for Wales It was an acknowledgment of this momentum, then, that the meeting was held in Cardiff, where Plaid Cymru recently ended a century of Labour control of the Senedd. Latest polling puts support for Wales to leave the UK at 32%, but growing in strength, and ap Iorwerth has been explicit that he won’t push for a referendum this term. Nevertheless, says Bethan, Plaid Cymru are “very ambitious … part of their agenda is to put Wales on the world map and mark Wales out as a nation that can stand on its own two feet.” Now in power , the party is focusing on domestic issues, and also bracing for disruption with Reform winning more than a third of seats in the Senedd. It’s a similar scenario at Holyrood, where Reform is joint second largest party alongside Scottish Labour. Both ap Iorwerth and Swinney have been outspoken in their opposition to right wing populism and benefited at the ballot box. There are already clear signs that Plaid Cymru has been learning from the SNP: one of their early priorities has been the Cynnal, a £10 a week child poverty payment, which is closely modelled on the successful Scottish Child Payment. … and Scotland The SNP was returned to Holyrood in May for an unprecedented fifth term, following a lacklustre campaign that mirrored voter disengagement and an unusually high level of undecideds. As its programme for government earlier this month failed to ignite public enthusiasm, this agreement is an opportunity for the Nationalists to “move the conversation back to their overarching aim - and have another confrontation with London,” Patrick Greenfield tells me. (He’s now reporting from Edinburgh, after a memorable stint on this very newsletter). Patrick reminds me that, while support for independence continues to hover around the 50% mark, enthusiasm among younger cohorts is higher: there’s a sense of Swinney future-proofing support for the party as Yes voters drift away from the SNP. And there’s the convenient diversion of attention from domestic travails, Patrick adds: the lingering scandal after former SNP chief executive Peter Murrell was jailed for embezzling party funds, demands for action as Scotland slumped in international education rankings last week, or looming public sector cuts as his government anticipates a near-£5bn gap in its finances by the end of the decade. Ahead of the Holyrood elections, I can recall Swinney positively beaming at the “seismic” potential of three pro-independence administrations: now it has come to pass, his focus is thought to be on seeking an agreed mechanism for triggering a vote, although that wasn’t discussed yesterday. But there is longstanding disagreement within the SNP about whether its better to build support for independence by doing the day job well rather than get lost in the weeds of referendum process. … and Northern Ireland Sinn Féin can talk up the significance of the memorandum but its focus is very much on next year’s Stormont assembly elections, Rory Carroll tells me from Dublin. Like the SNP, Sinn Féin’s popularity has slipped in recent years as public services crumble and it fail to deliver on key infrastructure pledges – but it is likely to win out against a fragmented unionist opposition. With support for Irish unity at 36% in Northern Ireland, Brexit hasn’t moved the dial decisively in favour, Rory says, while the Good Friday agreement is “famously murky and vague” on a precise mechanism that would trigger a poll. Does a “majority in favour” refer to opinion polls, elections or some other measure? Stormont has also become “so dysfunctional” that the narrative is growing stronger that Northern Ireland simply doesn’t work, Rory says. “That surely has to be bad news for unionism. So longer term, all bets are off because the status quo cannot continue indefinitely.” A resolution on devolution With devolution his guiding principle, Andy Burnham finds himself in a philosophical quandary. He could ape the more muscular unionism of the Starmer era, with senior Labour figures in Scotland and Wales punting devolution to local authorities as a means to sidestep the parliaments now seen as “captured” by nationalists. Or he could follow a more incremental approach, relinquishing further powers within the current constitutional framework. Wales is pressing for the devolution of justice; SNP proposals for a Scottish work visa to combat migrant worker shortages were rejected by Burnham’s government last month. Burnham has said he understands there’s a difference between devolution at regional and national level, but he has yet to set out precisely what he means by that. “Burnham didn’t impress because he didn’t seem to get what it already looked like to people in Scotland and Wales,” says Bethan. “There’s a whole generation that has grown up with institutions like Holyrood and the Senedd”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion The trouble is that, unlike No 10 in the North, a whole architecture of devolution already exists in the nations, that is essentially competing with Westminster over who gets to control what. After all, an independence referendum could be described as peak devolution. While Burnham still has to get to grips with this internal contradiction, the nationalist leaders have their eye on the arc of history. “I do think that maybe 20 years from now, we all might look back on this meeting in Cardiff and say that was an early step on a very clear path,” says Bethan. What else we’ve been enjoying View image in fullscreen Jeju SK’s Kim Jae-woo shows the effects of the hot conditions in South Korea. https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/09/27/oros.text: Menü Kereső Ukrajna lerohanása óta először tárgyalt német kollégájával az orosz külügyminiszter Külföld Vida Benjámin Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Szombaton New Yorkban, az ENSZ Közgyűlésének apropóján találkozott Szergej Lavrov orosz és Johann Wadephul német külügyminiszter – írta a Reuters . Ez volt az első ilyen megbeszélés azóta, hogy Oroszország 2022-ben megtámadta Ukrajnát. A találkozót Wadephul kezdeményezte, és közvetlenül azelőtt került rá sor, hogy Lavrov felszólalt az ENSZ Közgyűlésén. A Moszkva és Berlin közötti kapcsolatok az orosz invázió kezdete óta befagytak, a feszültség pedig tovább nőtt, miután augusztus elején egy közepes méretű drón repült be a lipcsei repülőtér területére, amin robbanószert is találtak . A lipcsei reptér egyébként stratégiai jelentőségű, mert rengeteg fegyverszállítmányt innen visznek Ukrajnába. A drón ott ért földet, ahol a legnagyobbat robbanhat egy megtankolt repülő, így már akkor biztos volt, hogy bárki állt is a háttérben, kemény üzenetet akart küldeni . A viszony elmérgesedését jelzi, hogy Szergej Lavrov egy sajtótájékoztatón azt mondta, a tárgyalások során semmi olyat nem tudott meg német kollégájától, amit Berlin korábban ne közölt volna már hivatalos nyilatkozataiban. „Őszintén megmondtam neki... egyszerűen felhívhatott volna, és azt mondhatta volna: »Olvassa el a nyilatkozatomat«” – fogalmazott Lavrov. A felek tisztviselői azonban közölték, hogy a miniszterek a kétoldalú kapcsolatokról és az ukrajnai háborúról is tárgyaltak. Egy német küldöttségi forrás szerint Johann Wadephul német külügyminiszter arra sürgette Lavrovot, hogy tegyen meg mindent annak érdekében, hogy megállapodás szülessen a Fekete-tengeren keresztül történő gabonaexportról. A találkozó ugyanis olyan diplomáciai erőfeszítések közepette valósult meg, amelyek célja Oroszország és Ukrajna fekete-tengeri gabona- és energiaexportjának újraindítása. Ezeket az exportokat jelentősen visszavetették a hajók és kikötői infrastruktúra elleni támadások. Lavrov elmondta, hogy Oroszország Indiával, Egyiptommal és Törökországgal is tárgyalt a Fekete-tengeren történő biztonságos hajózás garantálására vonatkozó javaslatokról. Ezek között olyan megoldások is lehetnek, amelyek Oroszország és az említett országok közötti kétoldalú megállapodásokon alapulnának. „Külön megbeszélésekre van szükség az ukránokkal, és nem kérések, hanem inkább követelések nyelvén” – mondta Lavrov, aki Ukrajnát hibáztatja a hajók elleni támadásokért. Ukrajna viszont kijelentette, hogy nyitott a megállapodásokra, és a háború minden következményéért az oroszokat, illetve az inváziójukat okolja. A német delegáció egyik forrása szerint Wadephul azt mondta Lavrovnak: Az idő sürget, tekintettel a számos országban, különösen a globális dél országaiban, tapasztalható élelmiszerhiányra, minden félnek késznek kell lennie arra, hogy konstruktívan vegyen részt a folyamatban. Az AP egy német delegációs tisztviselőre hivatkozva azt írta, Wadephul a találkozón felszólította Oroszországot, hogy hagyjon fel a Németországgal, Európával és a NATO-val szembeni „veszélyes eszkalációs pályával”. Lavrov az ENSZ Közgyűlésén mondott beszédében elutasította a német felszólítást, majd azzal vádolta Németországot, hogy Ukrajna fő támogatója, és arra törekszik, hogy Európa vezető katonai hatalmává váljon. „Berlin vajon érti, hogy mindez hová vezethet?” – kérdezte Szergej Lavrov orosz külügyminiszter az ENSZ Közgyűlésének éves ülésszakán. „Nem tanulták meg a második világháború leckéit?” Az orosz külügyminiszter beszédében és a találkozó utáni sajtótájékoztatón is elítélte a kollektív Nyugatot. Lavrov azt mondta, a Nyugat Oroszország stratégiai vereségét akarja elérni, „ezek a törekvések azonban oda vezetnek, hogy a háborúpártiak stratégiai zsákutcába kerülnek”. Azt is állította, hogy az Egyesült Államok lerombolta az európai biztonsági rendszert, és egy oroszellenes rendszert hozott létre Kijevben. Oroszország úgy véli, hogy Donald Trump és Vlagyimir Putyin 2025 augusztusi alaszkai találkozóján megállapodás született az ukrajnai háború befejezéséről – mondta Lavrov, hozzátéve, hogy továbbra is készen állnak visszatérni ehhez. Az orosz külügyminiszter egy igazságosabb, többpólusú világrend kibontakozásáról is beszélt az ENSZ Közgyűlésén. A meghiúsult lipcsei dróntámadásért Németország Oroszországot tette felelőssé . Oroszország alaptalannak minősítette a német vádakat, és azzal vádolta Berlint, bizonyítékokat hamisított, hogy Oroszországot felelőssé tegye a támadásért. Vlagyimir Putyin orosz elnök súlyos hibának nevezte, hogy Németország hozzájuk kötötte a lipcsei esetet. Oroszország a német lépésekre reagálva bezáratta a Goethe Intézet moszkvai, szentpétervári és jekatyerinburgi kirendeltségét . Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Helen Haines has been injured in an incident outside her office in Wangaratta, in regional Victoria. Photograph: Hilary Wardhaugh/Getty Images Helen Haines ‘Deeply appalled’: politicians condemn alleged attack after independent MP Helen Haines critically injured Anthony Albanese says his thoughts are with Indi MP after arrest of driver in Wangaratta Who is Helen Haines, the MP allegedly attacked in Victoria? What we know so far Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast Nino Bucci and Krishani Dhanji Mon 19 Oct 2026 07.10 EDT First published on Mon 19 Oct 2026 03.47 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The independent MP Helen Haines has been critically injured in an alleged attack involving a vehicle outside her electorate office in Wangaratta, in regional Victoria. The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, confirmed on Monday night that a man was in custody after the alleged attack on Haines that was now being investigated by the Australian federal police (AFP), Asio and the joint counter-terror taskforce. He said the motive for the alleged attack was not known, and would not comment on whether the suspect was known to police. Helen Haines is in a critical condition after an alleged attack. Here’s what we know so far Read more “Helen Haines is incredibly hard-working. She is fiercely intelligent, but most importantly, she’s just a thoroughly decent human being, full of integrity and respected right across the parliament, and from everyone who comes into contact with her, she is a well-loved member of her community, and this will come as an incredible shock to that community,” Albanese said. He said he respected her integrity most of all. “It doesn’t mean we always agree, but I always agree that her motives are good,” Albanese said. “Our thoughts remain with Helen Haines at this very difficult time.” View image in fullscreen ABC vision from the scene near where Helen Haines was allegedly struck by a vehicle. Photograph: ABC The prime minister and Victoria police said they were not aware of any recent direct threats to Haines. Albanese later said on the ABC’s 7.30 program that while he did not want to speculate on the motivation for the alleged attack, he had repeatedly warned “the temperature has increased in recent times” in relation to politics. He had feared that would increase the risk of political violence occurring in Australia that had been seen in other western democracies. Albanese, who became emotional at times during the interview, said he first was told that Haines had been injured in a car accident, before being informed it was allegedly a deliberate act. “This wasn’t an accident,” he said. Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, also said there had been an increase in threats towards politicians. “The year before last, we had 951 reports of harassing and threatening behaviour against various high officeholders,” he said. “The more recent financial year, that 951 has gone to 1,067.” ‘Our beloved Helen’ In a statement, Haines’s family confirmed that she had been injured and thanked bystanders for their assistance. “This afternoon, our beloved Helen was involved in an incident outside her Wangaratta Electorate Office, and is receiving medical care,” they said in the statement. “We thank the swift assistance of bystanders and the dedicated health workers who assisted her, and police for their response. “Our family, and Helen’s staff, will be making no further comment at this time, and ask that their privacy be respected by the public and media. “Please keep Helen in your thoughts.” Wangaratta map Haines was airlifted to hospital in Melbourne. In a statement, Victoria police said a 43-year-old man from Tarrawingee, about 10km from Wangaratta, was in custody and that a knife had allegedly been found in his car. They alleged he had been detained by a passerby when he exited the car. The statement said the woman that was struck was in a critical condition. “Police have arrested a man after a woman was struck by a vehicle in Wangaratta this afternoon. “It is understood a white Toyota LandCruiser struck the 65-year-old woman outside an office on Murphy Street about 3.35pm.” Police said that they were investigating as to whether it was an intentional act, and it was not known if “the parties are known to each other”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Politics, really Our political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for you after newsletter promotion Speaking at the scene, acting Supt Ashley Mason said it was being treated as an isolated incident. He said that the bystanders who assisted in the arrest and with Haines should be commended for acting as they did when confronted with a “horrific tragic incident”. It was a “dynamic incident” with an extensive crime scene, he said. ‘Deeply appalled’ The Victorian premier, Ben Carroll, said he knew the alleged attack would be devastating for the Wangaratta community and all those Haines represented. “I am deeply appalled by this [alleged] violent attack on Helen Haines,” he said in a statement. “My thoughts – and the thoughts of all Victorians – are with Helen, her family, her friends, her colleagues and her community.” The opposition leader, Angus Taylor, said the incident was a “shocking day for our nation”, and that political attacks cannot be normalised in Australia. Who is Helen Haines, the MP allegedly attacked in Victoria? Read more The Liberal leader said he was “deeply saddened and distressed” and was praying for Haines and her family. “This is a shocking day for our nation … Australians will be angry and appalled by the [alleged] attack on Helen outside her electorate office in Wangaratta,” he said in a statement on social media. In a social media post, theNationals MP Michael McCormack said it was “such awful news”. “Sending my love and best wishes to Helen Haines for a full and speedy recovery,” McCormack said. Police were expected to release a statement regarding the incident on Monday night. Haines has represented the electorate of Indi since 2019. ‘Politically motivated violence’ Asio has in recent years repeatedly warned about the rising threat of politically motivated violence . “Political differences, political debates and political protests are essential parts of a healthy democracy,” Mike Burgess, the Asio director general, said in 2025. “Unfortunately, here and overseas, levels of personal grievance and frustration are growing. “Rightly or wrongly some Australians feel dispossessed, disaffected, disenfranchised … many of the aggrieved do not necessarily espouse violent views, but may still see violence as a legitimate way to effect political or societal change.” He added last year that although Australia’s terrorism threat level remained at probable, the system was not “designed for a situation like the one we now face”. “We do know the environment is degrading and acts of politically motivated violence are becoming more likely than probable suggests,” he said. “Just as climate change increases the likelihood of extreme weather but does not forecast specific storms, politically motivated violence, including acts of terrorism, is more likely even though we cannot predict a specific attack.” Explore more on these topics Helen Haines Australian politics Victoria Independents Australian security and counter-terrorism news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Premier ‘deeply appalled’ after Indi MP Haines injured – as it happened ‘Everything you would want from a politician’: who is Helen Haines, the MP allegedly attacked in Victoria?
